title: ATTEMPTED MURDER
full_story:
A rural Fairfield man, Rawleigh L. Bailey, 53, was arrested on preliminary charges in connection with the shooting of his girlfriend, Becky Bennett, who was found alive with multiple gunshot wounds Sunday morning.  Bennett is currently being treated at Deaconess in Evansville, Indiana.

A media release Monday morning from the Wayne County Sheriff’s Office said a deputy was dispatched to Rawleigh Bailey’s residence at about 9 am Sunday to conduct a welfare check on Becky, who reportedly went to the home Saturday to retrieve items.

After family and friends had not heard from Becky on Saturday, a welfare check by the Wayne County Sheriff’s Office was requested Sunday morning.

While conducting the welfare check on Becky, deputies found her in a bedroom of the home with multiple gunshot wounds.  Deputies immediately took Rawleigh Bailey into custody and dispatched medical personnel who found she was still alive.

Rawleigh Bailey is currently being held at the Wayne County Jail and faces preliminary charges of attempted first-degree murder, domestic battery and aggravated discharge of a firearm.

title: INGRAHAM LABOR DAY PICNIC

title: COMMUNITY CHOIR REHEARSALS
full_story:
For 16 seasons, the Olney Central College Community Choir has brought together singers from across Southeastern Illinois to share their voices, build friendships and experience the joy of making music together.

OCC Director of Choral Activities Dr. Andrew Pittman invites new and returning singers to become part of the tradition when rehearsals begin at 6 pm on September 8th.

“There is something special about making music together,” he said.  “To share the joy of singing together and to experience that visceral sense of connection that happens when voices come together is truly unique.”

The choir offers an opportunity for fellowship and camaraderie while giving singers the chance to learn, grow and perform alongside others who share a love of music.  High school-age singers and older are welcome to participate, and no audition is required.  The only requirements are the ability to carry a tune and, most importantly, a desire to sing.

“I think one of the most rewarding things about the Community Choir is seeing people come in at the beginning of the semester and watching their confidence grow,” Pittman added.

Rehearsals will be held from 6 to 8 pm on Tuesdays in Room 216, the OCC Choir/Band Room, on the second floor of Dr. Kent L. Wattleworth Hall.  The choir will present its annual Christmas Concert at 7 pm on December 3rd in the Dr. John D. Stull Performing Arts Center.

To register for the OCC Community Choir, call 618-395-7777 as soon as possible.

title: FORD TOWN FUN FEST 2026
full_story:
Ford Town Fun Fest is coming up on Friday, September 18th and Saturday, September 19th.

The location for the festival is in front of the Flora Public Library and Food trucks will be set up on East 2nd Street.

The event starts with a Cruise in Friday from 5 pm, starting at the parking lot of Beck’s Auto Sales with dash plaques to the first 100 entries.  The car show is open to any make or model of car.  They will be cruising through town and past Heritage Woods so the residents can look at the vehicles.  Food trucks inflatables and family yard games will be available at Library Park from 5 to 8 pm, and Just for Spite Unplugged will be playing from 6 to 9 pm.

Saturday the Clay County Cruisers will have a Car Show with registration from 9 until Noon.  The car show registration is $15 and there will be awards for the top 75 plus 5 specialty awards.  For Car show information call 618-676-4005, 618-662-5646 or 618-676-7732.  Dash plaques will be given to the first 100 entrants.  Craft and food vendors, inflatables, and games will also open at 9 am.  There are also commemorative T-shirts available for $20.

title: ISP NITE PATROLS
full_story:
Illinois State Police (ISP) Troop 9 Commander, Lieutenant Bruce Waggoner, announced that the ISP will conduct Nighttime Enforcement (NITE) patrols in Clay, Fayette, Wayne, Effingham, Marion, White, and Hamilton counties during September.  NITE patrols allow the ISP to focus on preventing, detecting, and taking enforcement action in response to impaired driving and occupant restraint violations especially between the hours of 9:00 pm and 6:00 am.

The number of unrestrained drivers killed in traffic crashes is significantly higher at nighttime and combined with impaired driving means even more traffic deaths during these critical hours.

Officers working the enforcement patrols will be watchful for motorists who show signs of impaired driving, improper seatbelt and child restraint usage, speeding, distracted driving, and other Illinois Vehicle Code violations.

Alcohol and drug impairment are estimated to be a factor in more than 47% of all fatal motor vehicle crashes in Illinois.  Over half of all fatal crashes in Illinois occur at night.  The NITE program allows officers to work even harder at removing dangerous impaired drivers from the road and making sure everyone is buckled up.  This project is funded through the Illinois Department of Transportation.

title: CALLS FOR RESIGNATION
full_story:
State Representative Charlie Meier is calling for the resignation of Illinois Department of Human Services Secretary Dulce Quintero.  His call comes following what he calls a year of tumult at DHS, including “a horrific audit that outlined poor recordkeeping, abuse, and neglect” and the abrupt announcement that DHS would be drastically scaling back services at Choate Mental Health and Rehabilitation Center in Anna.

Meier noted the lack of accountability and oversight at all levels with DHS.  He cited several examples including people deemed unfit to stand trial sit in Illinois jails for months waiting for DHS to place them in a facility and abuse and neglect continuing to run rampant through Community Integrated Living Arrangements or CILA’s.

Meier says Governor Pritzker and Director Quintero have ignored the taxpayer funded study from SIU that outlined how Choate could continue to provide services for the state’s vulnerable residents.

Meier noted past practices of closures have “treated humans more like livestock than people, rounding them up and throwing them in buses at all hours of the night with no thoughts of how the move will impact the individuals or their families.”  He notes the agency even goes as far as to tell families that the only way their loved ones can receive services is to give up guardianship of them to the state.  Meier accuses the director of approving promotions for employees under DHS control despite their direct oversight of abuse in other CILAs and State Operated Developmental Centers.

Meier serves on the Illinois Legislative Audit Commission and is a member of the House Human Services committee.

title: FILE CLAIMS EARLY
full_story:
Illinois farmers have dealt with plenty of wind and hail damage this growing season, but excessive rainfall is driving a significant uptick in crop insurance claims.

Dylan Houser, crop claims manager for COUNTRY Financial, said wind and hail claims are running close to the company’s five-year average.  Early-season timing helped limit some of the damage from severe storms.

“The major weather events that came through northern Illinois early, Kankakee County with softball-size hail, crop was really small stage or not through the ground yet,” Houser told DeLoss Jahnke with the RFD Radio Network.  “That’s helped us.  We’ve been very fortunate there.”

Torrential rains and record rainfall in several counties have led to more replant claims and losses from flooding.  In some cases, farmers have replanted flooded areas only to see those same areas flooded again by additional rainfall.

Houser said that can lead to both a replant claim and potentially a production claim later in the season.

“If it floods out again, we’re not going to have production there,” he said.  “We’re probably going to be in a production claim situation.”

Houser shared several critical steps for managing losses, emphasizing farmers should submit a claim as soon as they suspect a loss to allow adjusters to document damage and provide guidance.

“If you think you’re going to have an issue, go ahead and get the claim in,” Houser said.  “There’s never a time where it’s too early to turn a claim in.”

Also, harvesting damaged acreage before an adjuster has appraised and measured it, and without consent, can result in denial of payments.

Houser encouraged farmers to report losses even if the damage appears limited to a single field.

“If you have any doubt, if you suspect any sort of loss, even if it’s at the field level, I’d get a claim in,” he said.

Farmers also have some additional flexibility with 60 more days to pay crop insurance premiums and the reinstated option to purchase an additional 5% prevented planting coverage.

USDA’s Risk Management Agency (RMA) is authorizing approved insurance providers (AIPs) to provide producers with up to 60 additional days to pay crop insurance premiums, administrative fees and amounts due under written payment agreements with scheduled premium billing dates this year between July 1st and September 30th.

During this extended period, AIPs may waive interest charges.  Interest will begin accruing for unpaid premium and administrative fees only after the end of the additional 60-day period or upon reaching the policy’s termination date, whichever occurs first.

Houser recommends farmers work with their insurance agent to understand how that flexibility applies to their operation.
